On Cloud, how long the page waits for Cloud's stored copy of your machine's Session summary to replay. It normally arrives at once; this keeps silence from blocking the page from asking the machine directly.
capacityRow.console.status_marker_retry_: Until then the list may be missing some Sessions; they fill in as updates arrive or at the next ask. Nothing for you to do.

On Cloud, when a freshly opened page lacks your machine's summary of which Sessions it has, how long it waits before asking again; a failed ask starts sooner and slows down to this. Waiting lets normal updates fill the gap instead of repeating requests through Cloud.
capacityRow.console.transcript_backoff_s: The page keeps retrying at this pace until a read succeeds, then returns to normal. If the conversation stays out of date, check that the machine and its network are up.

When reading a conversation fails, for example because the machine or network is down, the page waits longer before each retry, up to this long. This keeps a dead connection from being retried every few seconds and draining a phone's battery and data.
capacityRow.console.transcript_fill_page: Automatic loading pauses at the limit. Choose Load earlier messages to continue.
Earlier history pages read automatically while the conversation does not fill the screen. This bounds work on large raw records.
capacityRow.console.transcript_follow_fa: When it ends, checks slow to every few seconds until the follow period is over; replies still appear. Nothing for you to do.

Right after you send, the conversation checks for the reply every two seconds for this long, because a reply usually starts within it. Keeping it short stopped a phone from making dozens of reads for every message.
capacityRow.console.transcript_follow_la: Each time this interval passes the page checks again, so a reply can show up to this much later than it was written. Nothing for you to do.

After the first fast stretch following a send, how often the conversation checks for the reply for the rest of that period. A slower pace here saves a phone's data while a long reply is being written.
capacityRow.console.transcript_follow_se: After that the page goes back to its usual pace, and a reply still appears as soon as the conversation shows new activity. Nothing for you to do.

After you send a message, the conversation checks for the reply more often for this long, so the answer appears quickly. It ends so that a message with no reply does not keep a phone checking rapidly.
capacityRow.console.transcript_merged_ro: The next read replaces the page with the newest part of the conversation, so the oldest messages on screen may drop off. Nothing for you to do.

How many messages an open conversation may pile onto its page from small "what's new" reads before it starts that page over. Without it, a conversation left open for hours would keep growing in the browser's memory.
capacityRow.console.transcript_revision_: Clear incompatible history, read the newest page once, then retry the older page once. A second failure stays visible with manual retry.
Limits automatic recovery when a held older-page cursor belongs to an outdated native transcript revision.
capacityRow.console.transcript_safety_se: When the time is up the page simply rereads the whole page; a missed message or an expired picture shows up then. Nothing for you to do.

The longest an open conversation goes without rereading its newest page in full. In between it fetches only what was added, which saves data, but that can miss a change, so a full read happens at least this often.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_attemp: After the last try the report is dropped and counted on this page.
How many times this browser tries to upload one connection-health report.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_backof: The next try goes after this wait, with the same report.
The longest wait between two tries of the same connection-health upload.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_batch_: The rest wait for the next upload.
How many connection-health records this browser puts in one upload.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_body_b: A larger report is split; a single record that still does not fit is dropped and counted on this page.
The largest connection-health report this browser sends to Cloud in one upload.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_buffer: The oldest record is dropped and counted, so the newest evidence is kept.
How many connection-health records this browser keeps while they wait to be uploaded.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_coales: The upload then goes with whatever has gathered.
How long a first connection-health record waits for others before an upload starts.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_count_: A larger count is recorded as this number.
The largest count a connection-health record can state.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_elapse: A longer stage is recorded as this long.
The longest stage duration a connection-health record can state.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_hourly: Nothing more is sent until the hour turns.
How much connection-health data this browser uploads in one hour, retries included.
Nothing more is sent until the hour turns; the waiting records keep their own limit.
How many connection-health uploads this browser makes in one hour, retries included.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_reques: The upload is stopped and tried again later like a network failure.
How long one connection-health upload may take before this browser gives up on it.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_retry_: A longer request waits this long instead.
The longest wait this browser accepts when Cloud asks it to send connection health later.
capacityRow.console.viewer_health_send_e: Records that arrive sooner wait for the next upload.
The shortest time between two connection-health uploads from this browser.
capacityRow.coordinator.aliases.full: The oldest earlier holder is forgotten. A task it dispatched long ago may not route its completion notice to the current coordinator; the task's record itself is kept. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.coordinator.aliases.what: Earlier conversations that held this machine's coordinator role. They are remembered only so a task one of them dispatched can still report its completion to the current coordinator.
capacityRow.coordinator.bind_attempts.fu: After the last try the claim is refused and the old holder keeps the role. Close the old coordinator conversation or try again once it is clearly gone.
capacityRow.coordinator.bind_attempts.wh: How many times a conversation claiming the coordinator role retries when it cannot tell whether the current holder is still running, so two conversations never hold the role at once.
capacityRow.decisions.open.full: A new question is refused and the Session asking is told; none already open is dropped early. Each one closes by its due date, at most seven days, with the default it named. Answering some frees room.
capacityRow.decisions.open.what: How many questions Sessions have asked you and are still waiting on, each with a default answer and a due date. Past this many, the list stops being something you can answer.
capacityRow.deploy.health_seconds.full: When time is up the update is abandoned: the previous version is selected again and restarted. Check the update's output for why the new version didn't start.
capacityRow.deploy.health_seconds.what: How long Clawdline's Linux update tool waits for a newly installed version and its console to prove they work before giving up. The previous version stays selected meanwhile, so a broken update can't leave the machine without Clawdline.
capacityRow.devices.list.full: Pairing a new device or signing in with the password on a new browser is refused. Remove a device you no longer use, then try again.
capacityRow.devices.list.what: How many phones, browsers and other devices are paired with this machine. Each one is someone's access, so Clawdline never removes one on its own.
capacityRow.diagnostics.route_latency_sa: The oldest time is overwritten by the newest; the slowest time ever seen is kept separately. Nothing for you to do.
How many recent response times the diagnostics keep for each kind of request, used to show the typical and slow times. Keeping only recent ones holds memory steady however long the daemon runs.
Further kinds are added together under one "overflow" entry; every request is still answered normally, only its own line in the diagnostics is missing. Nothing for you to do.
How many kinds of request Clawdline's diagnostics keep separate counts and timings for. It stops unusual request addresses from each adding a new entry to memory.
capacityRow.dispatch.also_work_ids.full: This is a ceiling on one dispatch. One naming more is refused whole and nothing is started, never quietly trimmed; split the extra items into their own dispatches.
capacityRow.dispatch.also_work_ids.what: How many extra Board items one child task may carry beside its main item. A child delivers on one branch and lands once, so past a handful the items are really separate pieces of work.
capacityRow.epic.child_items.full: The Session's next child item is refused and nothing is created. Split the remaining work into a second Epic, or decide with the Session how to continue.
capacityRow.epic.child_items.what: How many child items an Epic's owner Session may break the Epic into, counting finished ones too. An Epic split into more pieces than this is really two Epics, and the ceiling also stops a looping Session.
capacityRow.handoff.pack_bytes.full: Once the total would pass it, further worktrees' changes are not saved; the note says so and asks the new owner to read those worktrees by hand. The reassignment still goes through.
capacityRow.handoff.pack_bytes.what: How large all the patches in one handoff note may be together when a Board item is reassigned. It stops one reassignment from writing a huge pile of patches to disk.
capacityRow.handoff.patch_bytes.full: This is a ceiling on one worktree. Changes larger than it are not saved; the note says so and points the new owner to that worktree to read by hand. The reassignment still goes through.
capacityRow.handoff.patch_bytes.what: How large one worktree's uncommitted changes may be for the handoff note to include them as a patch when a Board item is reassigned. A huge patch would make the note slow to write and hard for the new owner to read.
capacityRow.handoff.worktrees.full: Worktrees past it are listed with a note to read them by hand; the reassignment itself still goes through. Nothing for you to do unless the new owner asks.
capacityRow.handoff.worktrees.what: How many worktrees Clawdline reads when a Board item is reassigned from one Session to another and it writes a handoff note of the unfinished work. It keeps the handoff from stalling on a long list.
capacityRow.icons.request_bytes.full: The current version has no way to save an icon this way, so nothing reaches this ceiling. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.icons.request_bytes.what: How large one request to save a project icon may be. It is meant as a ceiling on a single save, so an oversized upload would be turned away before being read.
capacityRow.icons.saved.full: The current console no longer saves new icons here, so this count does not grow. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.icons.saved.what: How many project icons saved on this machine by earlier versions of Clawdline are kept. The file is read every time a project or Session list is drawn, so it must stay small.
capacityRow.icons.side.full: This is a ceiling on one icon, not something that fills up. A larger icon is refused, so that project's settings can't be applied until the source uses a smaller icon.
capacityRow.icons.side.what: How many cells wide or tall a project icon may be when it arrives from another machine through project settings sync. A ceiling keeps one icon from turning into a big picture sent with every list.
capacityRow.intent.cloud_wait_seconds.fu: When time is up the hosted console stops waiting and shows the request as failed; nothing is created. Try again.
capacityRow.intent.cloud_wait_seconds.wh: How long the hosted console on app.clawdline.com waits for this machine to answer a voice request to start work. It covers waiting behind another request, two attempts, and the trip through Cloud.
capacityRow.intent.planner_queue.full: A third request is refused as busy. Wait a few seconds for the current one to finish and press Start again.
capacityRow.intent.planner_queue.what: How many voice requests to start work can be handled at once: one being drafted by an assistant and one waiting. Each draft runs a Claude Code or Codex turn, so a pile-up would spend usage and slow the answer.
capacityRow.intent.planner_seconds.full: When time is up the turn is stopped and you are told the draft failed; nothing is created. Try again, or fill the form by hand.
capacityRow.intent.planner_seconds.what: How long one assistant turn may run when drafting a voice request, suggesting a role, or naming a Session automatically. A stuck command-line assistant would otherwise hold the queue forever.
capacityRow.intent.request_bytes.full: This never fills up. A longer request is refused before any assistant turn is spent; say or type it more briefly.
capacityRow.intent.request_bytes.what: How long a spoken or typed request may be when you use the microphone to start work or add a Board item, or describe a new role. It is a ceiling on one request, checked before an assistant is asked to read it.
capacityRow.intent.stderr_bytes.full: Older error output is dropped and only the end is kept; it is freed when the turn ends. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.intent.stderr_bytes.what: How much of a failed assistant turn's error output Clawdline keeps when drafting a voice request or naming a Session. It only needs the last lines to tell 'out of usage' apart from other failures.
capacityRow.iterm.osascript_kinds.full: Because the kinds are fixed, this does not fill in use. If it did, extra kinds would be counted together as other, so no run goes uncounted. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.osascript_kinds.what: How many kinds of iTerm2 commands (listing tabs, typing, capturing a screen, closing…) are counted separately in the diagnostics. The kinds are fixed in Clawdline itself.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_cooldown_seconds: Within this time a new run of timeouts writes no new diagnosis, though each failure is still logged. Nothing for you to do.
The least time between two iTerm2-freeze diagnoses. One freeze can last many minutes, and one diagnosis per episode is enough; more would only fill the logs folder.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_diagnoses.full: After a new one is written the oldest are deleted. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_diagnoses.what: How many diagnosis files about iTerm2 freezing are kept in Clawdline's logs folder. Each one records what iTerm2 was doing when it stopped answering, which helps track down the cause.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_failures.full: The oldest is dropped when a new failure arrives; every failure is still in the log. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_failures.what: The most recent failed attempts to talk to iTerm2, kept so that when iTerm2 stops responding, Clawdline can write a diagnosis of what happened. Each is already in the log, so only the latest few are needed.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_said_bytes.full: This is a ceiling on one message. Anything before the kept end is cut off; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_said_bytes.what: How much of iTerm2's error message is kept for one failed command in the log and in stall diagnoses. The end is kept because that is where the error number is.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_section_bytes.fu: This is a ceiling on one section. The rest is not written and the section says how much was left out; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_section_bytes.wh: How much of one step's output an iTerm2-freeze diagnosis may contain, such as a sample of what iTerm2 was doing. A ceiling keeps one diagnosis file from becoming huge.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_step_seconds.ful: A step that runs out of time is abandoned and marked as timed out, and the diagnosis goes on with the next step. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.stall_step_seconds.wha: How long one step of an iTerm2-freeze diagnosis may take. A step that hangs (iTerm2 is already not answering) must not stop the rest of the diagnosis.
capacityRow.iterm.viewer_concurrent.full: While one is still opening, a new Session starts normally but gets no iTerm2 tab; it is still usable in the console. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.iterm.viewer_concurrent.what: How many of those optional iTerm2 tabs for new tmux Sessions may be opening at once. A stuck iTerm2 would otherwise pile up waiting attempts when you start several Sessions quickly.
capacityRow.iterm.viewer_open_seconds.fu: If iTerm2 does not open the tab in time, the attempt is abandoned and logged; the Session works normally in the console, just without that iTerm2 tab.
capacityRow.iterm.viewer_open_seconds.wh: How long Clawdline tries to open an iTerm2 tab showing a Session you just started in tmux. The Session itself is already running, so this extra tab must never hold up the start.
capacityRow.leases.queue.full: A new Session asking to join is told the line is full and to retry later; nobody already in line loses their place. It will retry; you need not act.
capacityRow.leases.queue.what: How many Sessions may wait in line for one shared turn: the single build-and-test slot on this machine, or landing work into one checkout. Only one runs at a time so they do not overload the machine or collide.
capacityRow.log.daemon.full: The file is set aside and a new one begins; only the few newest old files are kept and older ones are deleted. You lose only old log history. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.log.daemon.what: The size of the Clawdline daemon's own log file, which records what it did and what went wrong. Without a ceiling it would keep growing on disk for as long as Clawdline runs.
capacityRow.memory.description_bytes.ful: This is a ceiling on one description. An entry with a longer one is refused before it is saved, and the Session is told; shorten the description.
capacityRow.memory.description_bytes.wha: How long one project-memory entry's one-line description may be. Every Session started in that project is given a list repeating each entry's description, so a long one costs every Session.
capacityRow.memory.entries.full: Adding another is refused and the Session that tried is told the memory is full. Ask a Session to forget entries that no longer apply, or remove them yourself, to make room.
capacityRow.memory.entries.what: How many entries one project's shared memory may hold: lessons that you or your Sessions recorded so later Claude Code and Codex Sessions in that project can read them. Each is someone's lesson, so none is dropped automatically.
capacityRow.memory.entry_bytes.full: This is a ceiling on one entry. Adding or editing one past it is refused before anything is saved, and the Session is told; shorten it or split it into several entries.
capacityRow.memory.entry_bytes.what: How long one project-memory entry's text may be. Sessions read these entries, so one very long entry would cost every Session that opens it.
capacityRow.memory.group_description_byt: This is a ceiling on one description, not something that fills up. A longer one is refused when the group is set; shorten it and set it again.
How long one memory group's 'read this when…' line may be. That line is repeated in the index every new Session on the project receives, so a long one makes every launch carry more.
capacityRow.memory.groups.full: Creating one more group is refused; existing groups and notes are untouched. Groups cannot be removed yet, so file new notes under an existing group or re-describe one.
capacityRow.memory.groups.what: How many groups one project's shared memory may sort its notes into. Every new Session on that project is handed a list naming every group, so too many groups would crowd out the notes themselves.
capacityRow.memory.name_bytes.full: This is a ceiling on one name. An entry with a longer name is refused before it is saved, and the Session is told; pick a shorter name.
capacityRow.memory.name_bytes.what: How long one project-memory entry's name may be. The name is also the entry's file name on disk, so it has to stay short.
capacityRow.naming.context_bytes.full: Older follow-up requests are left out first; the name is drawn from what remains. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.naming.context_bytes.what: How much of a conversation an assistant reads when it names a Session for you: the opening request, the latest requests that fit, and part of the latest reply. A ceiling keeps each naming turn cheap and quick.
capacityRow.naming.tail_entries.full: Older parts of the record are not read; the opening request is still used. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.naming.tail_entries.what: How far back in a conversation's record Clawdline looks when naming a Session automatically. Reading a long conversation's whole record for a short name would be slow.
capacityRow.notification.rule_label_char: This is a ceiling on one rule, not something that fills up. A rule with longer text is not accepted; shorten the name part.
How long the Session-name text a notification rule matches on may be. Session names are one short line, so a longer match text could never fire.
capacityRow.notification.rule_wait_secon: This is a ceiling on one rule, not something that fills up. A rule asking for a longer wait is not accepted; choose a shorter wait.
The longest a notification rule may wait before telling you a Session needs you. A rule that waits longer is closer to forgetting than to a reminder.
capacityRow.notification.rules_rows.full: Adding another rule is refused with a message that the limit was reached; your existing rules keep working. Delete a rule you no longer need first.
capacityRow.notification.rules_rows.what: How many custom notification rules you can keep, such as 'notify me when a Session named deploy needs my answer for 10 minutes'. Every waiting Session is checked against every rule, so the list stays short.
capacityRow.orchestrator.opening_stuck_s: When time is up that opening is marked failed with a timeout reason, so the item no longer looks busy. Assign or hand off the work again.

How long a Board item may show a new Session being opened and briefed, or a handoff being delivered, without any progress. Normally that takes minutes; if Clawdline stopped midway, the item would otherwise claim someone is being briefed forever.
capacityRow.personas.catalog.full: The list is fixed in each release and cannot grow while Clawdline runs. There is nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.personas.catalog.what: How many built-in roles (architect, reviewer, backend engineer…) Clawdline offers when you open a Session or assign Board work. A ceiling keeps the role picker short enough to choose from.
capacityRow.personas.suggestion_context_: The end of a long description is left out and the suggestion is based on the rest. Nothing is required, but put the key details early in the description.

When you ask for an AI role suggestion on a Board item, how much is sent to the assistant: the list of roles plus the item's title and as much of its description as fits. This caps what each suggestion costs.
capacityRow.personas.text_bytes.full: Roles ship inside Clawdline and are checked before each release, so this never fills while you use it. There is nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.personas.text_bytes.what: How long a single built-in role's instructions may be. A Session given a role reads that text on every turn, so a longer one makes every turn of that conversation cost more.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_history_b: A scan that reaches the byte limit is refused; provider records are not deleted.
Limits total native record bytes read for one history scan.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_history_e: An over-budget scan is refused instead of returning a misleading partial history.
Limits the native conversation directories and records inspected for one history read.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_history_m: A scan that exceeds the deadline is refused, preserving an honest unknown history.
Limits time spent on one native history scan.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_history_t: A longer fallback title is shortened with an ellipsis; the conversation stays intact.
Limits the fallback title derived from a conversation first line.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_probe_out: Oversized output makes the compatibility check fail. Clawdline will not launch that executable.
Limits the output retained while checking whether an installed Antigravity executable is the supported standalone CLI.
capacityRow.places.antigravity_probe_sec: If the probe times out, compatibility stays unknown and launch remains unavailable. No model request is made.
Limits each changed Antigravity executable compatibility probe. Draining output after cancellation has a separate limit of the same duration.
capacityRow.places.git_config_bytes.full: A larger settings file is skipped, so that project shows no origin: it can't sync settings to another machine, and moving its schedules elsewhere says it has no origin.
capacityRow.places.git_config_bytes.what: How much of a project's Git settings file Clawdline reads to learn which repository it comes from. A ceiling keeps one odd checkout with a giant settings file from slowing the project list.
capacityRow.places.registered.full: Adding or hiding another folder is refused. Remove projects or hidden folders you no longer need, for example with clawdline project remove, to make room.
capacityRow.places.registered.what: How many project folders you added by hand plus folders you chose to hide from the lists. Each entry is your own choice, so Clawdline never removes one by itself.
capacityRow.places.repo_lookups.full: The oldest remembered lookups are forgotten and read again when needed; at worst a project's origin appears a moment later. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.places.repo_lookups.what: How many projects' Git details (such as which remote they come from) Clawdline remembers so the project list doesn't have to re-read every repository each time it opens.
capacityRow.places.repo_readers.full: Further reads wait their turn; the project list still opens and those projects' origins appear later. If they never appear, check for a pending macOS permission prompt.
capacityRow.places.repo_readers.what: How many projects' Git settings Clawdline reads at the same time when filling in where each project comes from. If one read gets stuck, for example on a macOS permission prompt, the others can't pile up behind an unlimited number of stuck reads.
capacityRow.places.repo_wait_seconds.ful: When time is up the list appears without the missing origins; they fill in on a later refresh once the reads finish. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.places.repo_wait_seconds.wha: How long the project list waits for projects' Git origin details before showing what it already has. Reading a repository can stall on a slow disk or permission prompt, and the list shouldn't hang with it.
capacityRow.places.setup_age_seconds.ful: When time is up the next list read checks that project's files again, so a change you made appears within about that time. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.places.setup_age_seconds.wha: How long a project's setup badges are reused before being read again. Without a refresh, changes you make to a project's deploy or server setup would never show on the list.
capacityRow.places.setup_lookups.full: The oldest finished readings not on the current list are forgotten and read again when needed; at worst a project's badges appear a moment later. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.places.setup_lookups.what: How many projects' setup badges (icon source, deploy, servers, sync readiness) Clawdline remembers, so the project list doesn't reopen each project's files every time it is drawn.
capacityRow.places.setup_readers.full: Further reads wait their turn; the list still opens and those badges appear later. If they never appear, check for a pending macOS permission prompt.
capacityRow.places.setup_readers.what: How many projects' setup files Clawdline reads at the same time for the project list's setup badges. If one read stalls, for example on a protected folder, it can't multiply into many stuck reads.
capacityRow.places.setup_wait_seconds.fu: When time is up the list appears with some badges missing; they fill in on a later refresh. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.places.setup_wait_seconds.wh: How long the project list waits for new setup badge readings before answering with what it has. A protected folder can make a file open wait indefinitely, and the list shouldn't hang with it.
capacityRow.planreview.blocking_listed.f: This is a ceiling on one message. The rest are counted as and N more, and the full review stays on the review task; nothing is lost.
capacityRow.planreview.blocking_listed.w: How many blocking problems from a plan review are named when work on a Feature or Epic is held back until the plan is fixed. Naming a few keeps the message readable even when a review found dozens.
capacityRow.projectfiles.file_bytes.full: A larger file is shown as too large and can't be opened or saved there. Edit it in your own editor.
capacityRow.projectfiles.file_bytes.what: How large one text file may be to preview in the project file browser or open in the instruction and skill editor. A ceiling keeps a huge file from being pushed to your browser or phone.
capacityRow.projectfiles.list.full: The list stops and says it is incomplete; files past it are not shown there. The files themselves are untouched.
capacityRow.projectfiles.list.what: How many instruction and skill files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, skills, commands) a project's settings page lists. Each one is opened and checked when the page loads, so a ceiling keeps it from stalling.
capacityRow.projectfiles.scan_entries.fu: The folder's listing stops and says it is truncated, and the unify check reports that project as unknown rather than guessing. The files themselves are untouched.
capacityRow.projectfiles.scan_entries.wh: How many names Clawdline reads from one folder: a skills folder in project settings, or one folder in the project file browser. A ceiling keeps a folder with huge numbers of files from freezing the page.
capacityRow.projectfiles.skill_summary_r: Longer text is cut off in the list only; the file itself is unchanged. Nothing for you to do.
How much of a skill's or command's name and description the project settings page shows. A ceiling keeps one wordy skill from stretching the list.
capacityRow.projectfiles.tree_depth.full: This never fills up. A deeper path is refused and can't be opened in the browser; open it in your editor instead.
capacityRow.projectfiles.tree_depth.what: How many folders deep a path may go in a project's file browser. It is a ceiling on one request, so a pathological nesting is turned away before Clawdline walks into it.
capacityRow.projectfiles.tree_path_bytes: This never fills up. A path over it is refused and that file or folder can't be opened in the browser; open it in your editor instead.
How long a file or folder path may be when you open it in a project's file browser. It is a ceiling on one request, so an absurd path is turned away before Clawdline touches the disk.
capacityRow.projectfiles.write_bytes.ful: This never fills up. A save over it is refused as too large and the file on disk is unchanged; your draft stays in the editor.
capacityRow.projectfiles.write_bytes.wha: How large one save from the instruction and skill editor may be. It is a ceiling on a single save, so an oversized upload is turned away before it is read into memory.
capacityRow.projects.antigravity_consent: The consent request is too large; shorten it before trying again.
Maximum bytes in one Antigravity Project consent change.
The answer timed out; the change may have completed. Read current status before retrying the same operation.
Maximum time the website waits for an Antigravity Project consent response, including its body.
capacityRow.projects.folder_rows.full: The list stops early and says it is cut short. Type the folder's full path directly instead of picking it.
capacityRow.projects.folder_rows.what: How many subfolders the folder picker shows in one directory when you add a project, for example from your phone. A ceiling keeps one page quick to send and scroll even in a huge directory.
capacityRow.projects.workspace_metadata_: An oversized registration file is refused; linked-worktree membership remains unverified.
The maximum size of one Git registration file read to confirm which Project a working directory belongs to.
capacityRow.projectsync.clones.full: Asking for another clone is refused while the slots are busy. Wait for one to finish, then ask again.
capacityRow.projectsync.clones.what: How many repositories this machine may be cloning at the same time while syncing project settings. Clones use network and disk heavily, so a ceiling stops a big selection from starting them all at once.
capacityRow.projectsync.entry_bytes.full: Files that would push a project over its budget are not sent and are named as withheld; the receiving machine keeps its own copy. A request over the ceiling is refused.
capacityRow.projectsync.entry_bytes.what: How large one project's synced settings may be in total, file contents included, when sent to another machine. A ceiling keeps one project's transfer well inside what Cloud will carry in one go.
capacityRow.projectsync.file_bytes.full: A larger file is not sent and is named as withheld; the receiving machine keeps its own copy if it has one. Copy that file over yourself if you need it there.
capacityRow.projectsync.file_bytes.what: How large one local-only file (a skill, command, agent or CLAUDE.local.md) may be to travel when project settings sync to another machine. A ceiling keeps one big file from crowding out the rest.
capacityRow.projectsync.manifest_project: Projects past the ceiling are listed as skipped instead of offered, so they can't be picked for syncing. Nothing else is affected.
How many projects one machine offers when another machine reads its project settings for syncing. A ceiling keeps that offer small enough to carry through Cloud and show on one page.
capacityRow.projectsync.mirrored.full: Mirroring one more repository is refused. Detach projects you no longer need to follow (make them this machine's own again) to free room.
capacityRow.projectsync.mirrored.what: How many repositories this machine follows from another machine's project settings. The record is read on every apply and at startup, so it has to stay small.
capacityRow.projectsync.path_bytes.full: A file with a longer path is quietly left out of the sync. Rename or move it to a shorter path if you need it on the other machine.
capacityRow.projectsync.path_bytes.what: How long a file's path inside a project may be for that file to travel when project settings sync to another machine. A ceiling keeps odd or malicious paths from being written on the receiving machine.
capacityRow.projectsync.project_files.fu: Files past the ceiling are not sent and are named as withheld; the receiving machine keeps whatever copy it already has rather than deleting it.
capacityRow.projectsync.project_files.wh: How many local-only files (skills, commands, agents, CLAUDE.local.md) one project carries to another machine when its settings sync. A ceiling keeps one project from turning into a bulk file transfer.
capacityRow.proposals.open.full: A new proposal is refused and the Session that made it is told; nothing already waiting is removed early. Each waiting one leaves by itself after seven days and its work stays in that Session's to-dos. Answering some frees room.
capacityRow.proposals.open.what: How many proposals from Sessions can wait at once in the Board's To confirm area for your answer. Past this many, the list is longer than anyone will read, and unanswered ones would just pile up.
capacityRow.push.subscriptions.full: Turning on notifications on a new device is refused. Turn them off on a device you no longer use, then try again. A device that uninstalled or revoked permission is removed by itself.
capacityRow.push.subscriptions.what: How many devices have asked this machine to send them push notifications, one per device. Each is a standing request to be told, so none is dropped to make room.
capacityRow.release.app_relist_seconds.f: This is a check interval, not something that fills. In the rare case a remembered process number is reused by another program, the new app is swapped in at most this much later. Nothing else to do.
capacityRow.release.app_relist_seconds.w: While a new app version waits for you to quit the app, Clawdline remembers which processes belong to the open app and only asks whether they are still running. This is the longest it trusts that list before it looks at every process again.
capacityRow.release.app_swap_poll_second: This is a check interval, not something that fills. If you reopen the app faster than one check, you get the old app once more and the new one is swapped in the next time you quit. Nothing else to do.

How often Clawdline checks whether you have quit the app, when a new app version is downloaded and waiting. The app can only be replaced while it is closed, so a short interval catches a quick quit and reopen.
capacityRow.release.apply_follow_seconds: When time is up the command says it could not read the outcome and exits, but the update itself keeps going. Check the update panel later to see how it ended.
How long the `clawdline update --apply` command keeps watching an update in your terminal before it stops waiting. It is long enough for a full download plus the restart.
capacityRow.release.archive_entries.full: That download is rejected as unsafe, nothing of it is kept, and the update panel shows the update as failed. Your current version keeps running; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.archive_entries.what: How many files one downloaded Clawdline release may contain when it is unpacked. A real release has far fewer; the ceiling stops a damaged or malicious download from flooding the disk with files.
capacityRow.release.artifact_bytes.full: A release naming a larger file is refused before anything is downloaded and the update is marked failed; the version you are running is untouched.
capacityRow.release.artifact_bytes.what: How large one release file may be. A real release is far smaller; the ceiling stops a bad release description from making Clawdline download something huge onto your disk.
capacityRow.release.auto_apply_retry_sec: This is a check interval, not something that fills. The update starts at the first check that finds your Sessions idle; nothing for you to do.
How often an automatic update that is waiting because a Session is busy checks again whether your Sessions are idle. It lets the update go in soon after you stop working instead of hours later.
capacityRow.release.backups_kept.full: When a new copy is taken the oldest is deleted. Your current data is not touched; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.backups_kept.what: How many copies of Clawdline's data (Board, to-dos, settings) are kept from just before each update, so a bad update can be undone. Each copy is a full copy, so keeping them all would fill the disk.
capacityRow.release.boot_attempts.full: On the start past this count, the new version gives up and the update is rolled back to the version you had. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.boot_attempts.what: How many times a new version may start while its update has not yet settled. It stops a version that keeps crashing at startup from being restarted forever.
capacityRow.release.check_interval_secon: When time is up it checks again in the background; until then the version panel shows the last answer. Nothing for you to do.
How often an installed Clawdline checks whether a new release is out, besides once at startup. Checking every few hours finds releases quickly without asking the release site constantly.
capacityRow.release.check_jitter_seconds: This is not something that fills. It only shifts when the next check happens by a little; nothing for you to do.
The most random extra delay added to each update check, so machines started at the same moment do not all ask the release site at once.
capacityRow.release.download_timeout_sec: When time is up the download is abandoned, the partial file is removed and the update is marked failed; the version you are running is untouched. Try updating again later.
How long downloading one release file may take when installing an update. A download that stalls should not hold the update lock forever.
capacityRow.release.failed_versions.full: The oldest remembered failure is forgotten first, so a very old failed version could be tried again automatically. You can still install any version by hand; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.failed_versions.what: Which versions rolled back after an update, so automatic updates do not try the same broken version again and again.
capacityRow.release.fetch_timeout_second: When time is up that read is abandoned; the version panel keeps the last good answer and shows the error beside it. It tries again on the next check.
How long one read of a release's description, its signatures or the list of releases may take during an update check. A slow or stalled connection should not leave the check hanging.
If the new version has not come up in time, the update is rolled back to the version you had, and the update panel says it rolled back. Nothing for you to do.
How long Clawdline waits, after restarting into a new version, for that version's console to open and report which build it is. It decides whether the new version actually came up.
capacityRow.release.list_bytes.full: A list that large is treated as unreadable: that update check fails and the update panel shows why, and nothing is installed. It is retried at the next check; you don't need to do anything.
capacityRow.release.list_bytes.what: How large GitHub's list of Clawdline releases may be when a beta-channel machine looks for its newest version. A ceiling stops a broken or hostile answer from being read into memory whole.
capacityRow.release.lock_stale_seconds.f: Until the marker is this old, starting another update is refused as already in progress; after that it is taken over and the update goes ahead. You only need to wait.
capacityRow.release.lock_stale_seconds.w: How old the marker saying an update is in progress must be before Clawdline assumes the process that left it died. It keeps two updates from running at once.
capacityRow.release.manifest_bytes.full: A larger list is refused as malformed and nothing in it is followed, so no update is offered from it; the version panel shows the error. Your running version is not affected.
capacityRow.release.manifest_bytes.what: How large the signed list describing a Clawdline release may be when an installed Clawdline checks for updates. The real one is small; the ceiling stops a broken or hostile download from using memory.
capacityRow.release.pending_deadline_sec: If the new version starts after this deadline it gives the update up and steps aside so the previous version starts again; the update panel shows it rolled back. Nothing for you to do.
How long one update may stay half-finished. It stops a machine from being left indefinitely between the old version and the new one.
capacityRow.release.previous_releases_ke: Older versions beyond these are deleted after a successful update; a version built from your own source checkout is never deleted. Nothing for you to do.
How many older Clawdline versions stay on disk after a successful update, so you could go back to one by hand. Each version takes real disk space.
capacityRow.release.signature_bytes.full: A larger file is refused as an invalid signature, so that release is not trusted or offered; the version panel shows the error. Your running version is not affected.
capacityRow.release.signature_bytes.what: How large the signature file that proves a release is genuine may be. It only needs to hold a few signatures, so anything bigger is treated as suspect.
capacityRow.release.smoke_timeout_second: If it does not answer in time the update is marked failed and nothing is switched; you keep the version you were running. Nothing for you to do.
How long Clawdline gives a newly downloaded version to answer a quick self-test before switching to it. It catches a version that cannot even start on this machine before anything changes.
capacityRow.release.state_file_bytes.ful: A file this large is reported as unreadable rather than taken to mean nothing is happening, so updating stops and says why. These files stay tiny in normal use; you would not see this unless one is damaged.
capacityRow.release.state_file_bytes.wha: How large one of the updater's own small record files (update status, pending update, failed versions, lock) may be. A ceiling stops a corrupted file from being read whole.
capacityRow.release.supervisor_runs.full: Past it the helper stops trying the new version and rolls back to the one you had; the update panel says so. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.supervisor_runs.what: How many times the helper that carries out one update may be started over. It stops an update that keeps getting interrupted from looping without end.
capacityRow.release.unpacked_bytes.full: That download is rejected as unsafe, nothing of it is kept, and the update panel shows the update as failed. Your current version keeps running; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.release.unpacked_bytes.what: How much disk space one downloaded Clawdline release may take once unpacked. The ceiling stops a damaged or malicious download from filling your disk while it is being unpacked.
capacityRow.run.claimed_items.full: This is a ceiling on one message. The next claim is refused and nothing changes; send another message if you want it to take on more.
capacityRow.run.claimed_items.what: How many Board items a Session may take on, or hand to a new Session, on the strength of one message from you. It stops one instruction from turning into a sweep that grabs half the Board.
capacityRow.run.created_items.full: This is a ceiling on one message. The Session's next item is refused and nothing is written; send another message if you really want more, or ask for one planning item.
capacityRow.run.created_items.what: How many Board items a Session may create on the strength of one message from you. A message asking for more is really a plan, and the ceiling stops a looping Session from flooding the Board.
capacityRow.schedule.run_transcript_head: This is a ceiling on one read. If the first message lies past it, that run is not matched and shows no Resume button; the conversation file is untouched. Nothing for you to do.
How much of the start of a conversation file Clawdline reads to find its first message when matching a scheduled run to the conversation it started.
capacityRow.schedule.run_transcripts_pro: This is a ceiling on one lookup. Older conversations are not opened, so a run among them shows no Resume button. You can still find that conversation yourself.
How many of a project's recent conversations Clawdline opens to match finished scheduled runs to the conversation each one started, for the run history and its Resume button.
capacityRow.screens.capture_slots.full: No extra capture is started; the row shows the last screen it already had, so a line may be a few seconds old. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.screens.capture_slots.what: How many terminal screen captures the Session list may run at once to refresh each row's latest line and menu. On iTerm2 every capture waits behind the same lock as your own keystrokes, so more at once would make typing lag.
capacityRow.session.close_scheduled.full: A further request is refused and that Session stays open; the assistant is told so and can ask again later, or you can close the Session yourself. A daemon restart also drops all waiting requests.
capacityRow.session.close_scheduled.what: How many Sessions may be waiting to close themselves once their current turn ends, after an assistant asked to close its own Session while still working. These requests live only in memory.
capacityRow.session.close_scheduled_per_: A repeat gets the same answer as the first and adds nothing; the Session still closes once, when its turn ends. Nothing for you to do.
How many pending close requests one Session's terminal may have. Asking again for the same Session is the same request, so repeats do not stack up.
capacityRow.session.close_scheduled_seco: When time is up and the Session is still working, the close request is dropped and the Session stays open; the assistant can ask again, or you can close it yourself.
How long a Session's request to close itself waits for its turn to finish. A turn that runs on and on should not leave a forgotten close that fires much later, at a surprising moment.
capacityRow.session.codex_past_page.full: Load older sessions follows the next page. Background records may be filtered out; failed reads can be retried without losing loaded sessions.
capacityRow.session.codex_past_page.what: How many Codex history records are requested for one page, so opening the picker does not wait for the whole project history.
capacityRow.session.direct_todo_bytes.fu: This is a ceiling on one to-do. A longer one is refused with a message saying it is too large, and nothing is added; shorten it or put the detail in a Board item.
capacityRow.session.direct_todo_bytes.wh: How long one to-do sent to a Session may be; the same ceiling applies to the reason on a work proposal. A Session reads its to-dos on its turns, so one huge to-do makes those turns slow and costly.
capacityRow.session.direct_todos.full: Adding another to-do to that Session is refused with a message saying it is full; nothing is dropped. Mark done or delete some of its open to-dos, then add again.
capacityRow.session.direct_todos.what: How many unfinished to-dos one Session can hold, whether you sent them or the Session wrote them for itself. Each one is something the Session is reminded of, so an endless list would bury the ones that matter.
capacityRow.session.executions.full: Closed conversations give back their entries by themselves. If it ever fills, sending to conversations from the phone is refused until some conversations are closed; old entries are never dropped silently.
capacityRow.session.executions.what: How many conversations on this machine Clawdline keeps an identity for, so a message sent from the phone reaches the exact program it was meant for, not a new one that reused the same terminal.
capacityRow.session.human_intervention_d: This is a ceiling on one Note. A Session whose detail is longer has the whole Note refused; for something long it should attach a Cloud document link instead.
How long the optional longer detail on a Note may be. The detail is stored with the Note and sent to the phone, so a ceiling keeps one Note from carrying a whole document.
This is a ceiling on one link. A Note with a longer link is refused whole and the Session must fix the link; you don't need to do anything.
How long the Cloud document link attached to a Note may be. A real link is short, so the ceiling only stops something that is not a proper link from being stored.
This is a ceiling on one suggestion. A Note with a longer one is refused whole and the Session must shorten it; you never see a cut-off suggestion.
How long each suggested reply on a question Note may be. You can edit a suggestion before sending it, so it should be a reply, not an essay.
capacityRow.session.human_intervention_t: This is a ceiling on one piece of text. A Session's Note with a longer field is refused whole and it must shorten it; if your resolution note is too long, saving it is refused with a message saying so.
How long a Note's summary, the action it asks of you, and its reason may each be, and also how long your own resolution text may be. Keeping these short makes a Note answerable in a few seconds.
This is a ceiling on one Note, not a container. A Session that writes a longer title has the whole Note refused and must shorten it; you never see a half-written Note.
How long one Note's title, or one suggested reply's label on it, may be. It keeps a Note readable at a glance in the list and on the phone.
capacityRow.session.human_interventions_: That Session cannot leave you a new Note, and a resolved one cannot be reopened, until you resolve one of its open Notes. Answer or close a few, and it can ask again.

How many unresolved Notes (questions, requests and handoffs a Session leaves for you) one Session can have open at once. It keeps a Session from flooding you with requests faster than you can answer them.
Older resolved Notes simply aren't listed; they are still kept until the overall history ceiling removes them. Nothing for you to do.
How many already-resolved Notes are shown beneath a Session's open ones. A short tail of recent answers gives you context without making the Notes list long to load or scroll.
Each new Note quietly removes the oldest resolved one, so very old answered Notes disappear from history. Open Notes are never removed. You don't need to do anything.
How many Notes, open and resolved together, Clawdline keeps across every Session. Resolved Notes are kept as history, and a ceiling keeps that history from growing forever in the database.
After this long without movement the conversation is marked quiet; nothing is stopped or closed. A conversation whose state cannot be read is never marked quiet.
How long a conversation's record may go without changing before the all-machines list in Cloud marks it as having no recent movement. It says nothing about whether the work is done.
capacityRow.session.report_open_todo_cha: This is a ceiling on one line. Longer text is cut off with an ellipsis in the reminder only; the full to-do is unchanged.
How much of each unfinished to-do's text the end-of-turn reminder repeats. A short one-line preview is enough for the Session to recognize it.
capacityRow.session.report_open_todo_row: This is a ceiling on one report. Extra to-dos are left out of the reminder and the report says the list was cut short; nothing is removed from the Session's to-do list.
How many unfinished to-dos the end-of-turn report reminds a Session of, among those it has already been sent. A long list here would crowd out the report itself.
capacityRow.session.secret_handoff_bytes: This is a ceiling on one value. A longer one is refused when you submit it, with a message that it is too large for Secret Handoff, and nothing is kept.

How large one value you paste into a Secret Handoff (a password, token or key handed to a Session without entering the conversation) may be. Values are held only in memory until used, so a ceiling keeps them small.
capacityRow.session.secret_handoff_deliv: When time is up the hand-off fails and the value is already used up, so it cannot be retried. Ask the Session to create a new Secret Handoff and paste the value again.

How long Clawdline waits to hand a Secret Handoff value to the Session's local command once it asks for it. The hand-off happens on this machine only, so a few seconds is enough, and a stalled receiver must not hold the secret open.
capacityRow.session.secret_handoff_pendi: Submitting another value is refused with a message to try again later. Waiting values clear by themselves when a Session uses them or when they expire.
How many pasted Secret Handoff values, across all Sessions, can wait in memory for their Session to pick them up. It stops secrets from piling up in memory where nothing collects them.
capacityRow.session.secret_handoff_secon: When time is up the value is wiped and the Session can no longer get it. Paste it again in the same Note when the Session is ready; restarting Clawdline also wipes waiting values.
How long a value you pasted into a Secret Handoff waits in memory for its Session to pick it up. A secret nobody collects should not linger, so it is wiped after this time.
capacityRow.session.title_age.full: A name set this long ago is dropped and the Session shows its automatic name again. Rename it again if you still want it.
capacityRow.session.title_age.what: How long a Session name you set by hand is kept. A terminal can outlive many conversations, and an old name must not end up labeling a later conversation in the same terminal.
capacityRow.session.title_characters.ful: This is a ceiling on one name, not something that fills up. A longer name is refused with a message; shorten it and save again.
capacityRow.session.title_characters.wha: How long a Session name you type may be, after line breaks and extra spaces are tidied. A name is shown on one line in lists and on the phone, so a ceiling keeps it readable.
This is a ceiling on one request, not something that fills up. An oversized rename is refused and the old name stays.
How large one request to rename a Session may be. A name is one short line, so a ceiling turns away an oversized request before it is read or copied into your settings file.
capacityRow.session.title_rows.full: Saving a new name forgets the oldest one, and that Session goes back to its automatic name. Rename it again if you still need it.
capacityRow.session.title_rows.what: How many Session names you set by hand Clawdline remembers. They live in your settings file, which is read every time the Session list is drawn.
capacityRow.session.todo_batch_rows.full: This is a ceiling on one batch. A larger batch is refused whole and nothing is added; the Session can send it in smaller parts.
capacityRow.session.todo_batch_rows.what: How many to-dos a Session may write for itself in one go, which it does only when you asked it to. A ceiling stops a Session that misread you from filling its list in one step.
capacityRow.session.waiting_for.full: The first ones are named and the row counts the rest it left out. The waiting itself is unaffected. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.session.waiting_for.what: How many tasks a waiting conversation names as what it is waiting for, so a lead Session with many children still fits on one row.
capacityRow.sessions.activity_reads.full: Sessions past the limit are not checked and are marked unread rather than quiet, so they sort ahead of ones with a known time in the same state. Nothing for you to do; closing Sessions you no longer need reduces it.
capacityRow.sessions.activity_reads.what: How many Sessions one refresh of the list checks for their last activity time, used to order the list. Each check is cheap, but a machine with a great many Sessions must not make every refresh slow.
capacityRow.sessions.agent_rows.full: The newest running ones are shown and the row says how many more were left out. Nothing is stopped. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.sessions.agent_rows.what: How many background agents (sub-agents a Session started) are shown under one conversation row, so a conversation running many of them still fits on one line.
capacityRow.sessions.archive_restore_bat: A request naming more is refused whole and nothing opens. Select fewer and restore them in several rounds.
How many archived Sessions one restore request may reopen at once. Each one starts an assistant, so a ceiling stops a single press from launching a flood of them.
capacityRow.sessions.archive_rows.full: The Session archived longest ago drops off the archive list. Its conversation is still in the assistant's own history and can be resumed from the project's past list while it appears there.
capacityRow.sessions.archive_rows.what: How many archived Sessions Clawdline remembers so you can bring them back later. Each one is a row you asked to keep, and the archive list has to stay quick to load and scroll.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_batch.full: A request naming more is refused whole and nothing opens. Select fewer conversations and restore them in several rounds.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_batch.what: How many conversations one 'restore after reboot' request may reopen at once. Each one starts an assistant, so a ceiling stops a single press from launching a flood of them.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_boots.full: On each new boot the oldest record is dropped by itself. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_boots.what: How many machine boots Clawdline keeps a record of open conversations for: the current one and the one before it. Only the previous boot's conversations can be offered back, so older records would only take space.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_grace.full: A conversation that went earlier than this window is not offered; its record stays until that boot's record is dropped. A tab you closed by hand just before rebooting may be offered, and you can dismiss it.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_grace.what: How long before the machine went down a conversation may have closed and still be offered back after the reboot. A shutdown closes apps over a few moments; conversations you closed well before that should not come back.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_heartbeat.f: When this time is up, the next check updates that one timestamp. Nothing visible changes and there is nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_heartbeat.w: How often Clawdline notes that this boot is still running while nothing else changes. After a reboot, that last note marks when the machine went down, which decides which conversations are offered back.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_rows.full: The conversations that have been idle longest are left out of the record, so they won't be offered back after a reboot; you can still resume them from the project's past list.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_rows.what: How many open conversations Clawdline writes down for this boot, so that after a reboot or crash it can offer them back. A ceiling keeps that record small even on a machine with very many open terminals.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_seen_age.fu: When this time is up, the next check rewrites the same list with the new time. Nothing visible changes and there is nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.sessions.restore_seen_age.wh: How long the 'last seen open' time on each recorded conversation may lag while nothing changes. Rewriting it on every check of the machine would mean a disk write every few seconds for no new information.
This is a ceiling on one view, not stored data. Past it, the oldest part is left out and the panel says the output was cut; the file itself stays whole. Nothing for you to do.
How much of a background command's output the Shell panel shows at once. The output file can be huge, so only its end is sent to the page.
This is a ceiling on one change, and normal settings are far smaller. A change over it is refused and your settings stay as they were.

How large one settings change may be, from the Settings page here, notification rules, or the default-model change sent from Cloud. A ceiling turns away an oversized request before it is copied into your settings file.
capacityRow.snippets.scope.full: Adding one more to that group is refused, the same way as the overall limit; the reading names the fullest group. Delete or move snippets out of that group to make room.
capacityRow.snippets.scope.what: How many snippets one group may hold: the snippets for every project, or those for a single project. A list longer than this in one sheet is already more than anyone scrolls through.
capacityRow.snippets.total.full: Adding one more is refused and the snippet sheet says the limit is reached. Delete snippets you no longer use to make room.
capacityRow.snippets.total.what: How many saved snippets (常用句) this machine holds across all projects, the reusable text you drop into a Session's input box. Each one is text you wrote, so Clawdline never deletes one on its own.
capacityRow.squad.body_bytes.full: Saving a longer one is refused as too large and nothing is saved. Shorten it and save again.
capacityRow.squad.body_bytes.what: How long one role's text, one skill (including its attached files) or one project handbook may be. Each is handed to the assistant in Sessions that use it, so this keeps one piece from bloating all of them.
capacityRow.squad.console_active_skill_b: The Squad page refuses to enable the skill and says the enabled skills together are over the safe limit. Disable another skill or shorten one, then try again.

The combined size of every skill switched on for one role, checked on the Squad page when you enable another. It sits below the start-up ceiling so a role cannot be saved with skills that would make every Session started with it fail.
capacityRow.squad.entities.full: Saving or importing more is refused with "The squad store is full." Clawdline has no way to delete saved versions yet, so there is nothing you can clear yourself.
capacityRow.squad.entities.what: How many saved roles, teams and skills the Squad catalog on this machine holds, counting every saved version. Each edit keeps the earlier version so Sessions and projects pinned to it keep working, so the count grows with every save.
capacityRow.squad.event_body_bytes.full: A larger report is refused and not recorded; that skill use simply is not shown. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.squad.event_body_bytes.what: The size of one report an assistant sends when it uses a skill. Real reports are tiny; the ceiling stops a misbehaving Session from sending the daemon a huge one.
capacityRow.squad.event_id_bytes.full: A report with a longer label is refused and not recorded, so that skill use is not shown. Assistants use short labels, so this does not happen in normal use. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.squad.event_id_bytes.what: The length of the label an assistant attaches when it reports using one of its role's skills, so a repeated report is recognised and counted once. The ceiling stops one report from storing an arbitrarily long label.
capacityRow.squad.event_page_rows.full: Nothing is lost: the remaining reports come in the next batch. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.squad.event_page_rows.what: How many skill-use reports are fetched in one go when catching up, for example after reconnecting. Fetching in batches keeps a long backlog from arriving as one oversized answer.
capacityRow.squad.launch_skill_when_rune: A longer line is cut and ends with an ellipsis; the assistant can still read the full skill when it needs it. Nothing for you to do.

How long the "when to use this skill" line may be that Clawdline quotes for each skill in the instructions a role's Session starts with. It keeps a long or hostile custom skill from filling those instructions.
capacityRow.squad.place_lookup.full: Projects beyond it are not offered in that list; settings already saved for them still appear, labelled by their ID. Nothing to do unless a project you need is missing.
capacityRow.squad.place_lookup.what: How many projects the Squad page looks through when you pick a project to give its own role settings. It keeps that list quick on a machine with very many folders.
capacityRow.squad.receipts.full: Further saves and imports are refused with "The squad store is full." These records are never cleared today, so there is currently nothing you can remove.
capacityRow.squad.receipts.what: Every change saved on the Squad page and every package import leaves a record, so a save that is retried is applied only once. This counts those records.
capacityRow.squad.recovery_page_rows.ful: Nothing is refused: the rescan reads the next batch until it has covered them all. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.squad.recovery_page_rows.wha: Sessions started with a role that Clawdline has not yet matched to their conversation, read in batches of this size when it rescans. Batching keeps one rescan from loading every pending start at once.
capacityRow.squad.request_bytes.full: A larger change is refused as too large and nothing is saved. Save it in smaller pieces, for example one role or skill at a time.
capacityRow.squad.request_bytes.what: How large one change sent from the Squad page may be, from this machine or through Cloud. It bounds what the daemon reads into memory for a single save.
capacityRow.squad.settings_rows.full: A new override is refused with "The squad store is full," while changing an existing one still works. Restoring a setting to inherit does not remove its entry, and there is no way to delete these yet.
capacityRow.squad.settings_rows.what: How many role settings are saved on this machine: each role's global or per-project override, such as a handbook, skill choices or auto-assignment, is one. Every project you customise a role in adds more.
capacityRow.squad.skill_source_summary_r: A longer description is cut off in the list; the skill itself is unchanged and its full text shows when you preview it. Nothing for you to do.
How long a skill's name and description may be in the Squad page's list of skills found in your projects and provider folders. Clipping keeps one skill with a huge description from swamping the list.
capacityRow.squad.snapshot_bytes.full: That Session is not started and nothing is saved; the message says the role, handbook and skills are too large for this machine. Disable some skills or shorten the handbook, then start again.
capacityRow.squad.snapshot_bytes.what: When you start a Session with a role, Clawdline saves a fixed copy of everything it is given: the role's text, the handbook and the full text of each enabled skill. The ceiling keeps one start from storing and handing the assistant an oversized bundle.
capacityRow.squadpackage.archive_bytes.f: The page says the package exceeds the limit and nothing is read or imported. Ask for a smaller package or split it into several.
capacityRow.squadpackage.archive_bytes.w: How large a squad package (a ZIP of shared roles, teams and skills) may be when you preview or import it. Packages hold short text, so this rejects anything far bigger than a real one before it is opened.
capacityRow.squadpackage.entries.full: The whole package is refused and nothing is imported. Ask the author to split it into smaller packages.
capacityRow.squadpackage.entries.what: How many files a squad package may contain. It stops a package made of thousands of tiny files from tying up the import.
The whole package is refused and nothing is imported. Ask the author for a smaller package.
How much a squad package may contain in total once unpacked. A small ZIP can unpack into a huge amount of data; this stops one from filling the machine's memory.
capacityRow.squadpackage.expansion_ratio: The whole package is refused and nothing is imported. Do not use that package; ask its author where it came from.
How many times larger than its compressed size a file in a squad package may unpack to. Text compresses only modestly; an extreme ratio is the mark of a ZIP built to exhaust memory.
capacityRow.squadpackage.file_bytes.full: The whole package is refused and nothing is imported. Ask the author to shorten or remove that file.
capacityRow.squadpackage.file_bytes.what: How large any single file inside a squad package may be once unpacked. Roles and skills are short text, so this catches a package that hides a large file.
The whole package is refused and nothing is imported. Ask the author for a corrected package.
How large a package's table of contents, the file listing every role, team and skill inside, may be. It keeps a malformed package from making Clawdline parse a giant index.
capacityRow.squadpackage.preview_age.ful: After that, importing says the preview expired and asks you to preview again. Preview the package again, then import.
capacityRow.squadpackage.preview_age.wha: How long a package preview stays valid for importing. An import must match what you reviewed, so an old preview is not trusted once the catalog may have changed.
capacityRow.squadpackage.preview_rows.fu: A new preview is refused with "The squad store is full" until older previews expire, within a quarter of an hour. Wait a few minutes and preview again.
capacityRow.squadpackage.preview_rows.wh: How many package previews can be waiting at once. You must preview a package before importing it, and each preview is kept for a while, so this stops repeated previews from piling up in the store.
capacityRow.squadpackage.request_bytes.f: The request is refused before anything is opened. A package within its own size limit always fits, so in practice you will not hit this. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.squadpackage.request_bytes.w: How large one package preview or import request may be; it carries the ZIP encoded as text. It stops the daemon from reading an oversized upload into memory.
capacityRow.sse.screen_pending.full: Past it, the page's live connection is closed and it reconnects, reading every screen afresh. You may see the page blink or reload its screens. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.sse.screen_pending.what: How many terminal screens with unsent updates one open Clawdline page may have waiting. A slow page keeps only the newest picture of each screen, so it is late but never wrong.
capacityRow.store.antigravity_consent_id: An oversized or malformed identity is refused before changing consent or writing a receipt.
The byte limit for each actor, request key and operation identity in an Antigravity consent request. An actor label alone does not authenticate a person.
capacityRow.store.antigravity_consent_ro: An oversized root is refused before changing consent or writing a receipt.
The byte limit for the canonical local Project root in an Antigravity consent request.
capacityRow.store.antigravity_project_co: New Projects are refused when full. Existing Projects can still revoke consent; no consent record is evicted automatically.

Local Antigravity Project hook consent records, including pending preparations and disabled records that preserve revocation revisions. Consent is never imported from repository files or workspace trust.
capacityRow.store.db.full: Today nothing is refused when it is full; the only effect is that Clawdline reports itself unhealthy on the status page. Check what is growing before it fills the disk.
capacityRow.store.db.what: The size of Clawdline's main database, which holds your Board items, dispatched task records and their landings. The ceiling sits far above normal use, so reaching it means something is writing far more than it should.
capacityRow.store.done_effect_retention_: This is an age, not something that fills. Older successful records are cleared a little at a time; the latest one for each notification and each paused Session stays. Nothing to do.
How long Clawdline keeps the record of a finished background step (a message typed, a tab closed, a notification sent) once it succeeded. Failed or uncertain steps are kept.
capacityRow.store.events.full: Past the ceiling the oldest rows are deleted first, even ones younger than two weeks. Nothing you see depends on them; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.store.events.what: How many rows Clawdline's journal of what happened keeps: tasks moving, pushes sent, sessions closing. Rows older than two weeks are deleted, except the newest one per session that Clawdline still reads back, which goes once that session has been silent for thirty days.
capacityRow.store.read_connections.full: Further reads wait their turn, so a page may load a little slower under heavy use; one that waits too long gives up and shows a load error you can retry. Saving is never held up by this.
capacityRow.store.read_connections.what: How many reads of Clawdline's data (Board, to-dos, history) can run at the same time, separately from writes. It keeps pages from waiting behind a save, without opening an unbounded number of database connections.
capacityRow.store.receipt_tombstone_rete: This is an age, not something that fills. After it, the memory of an old request is cleared, so a command retried with the same --key more than a week later runs again. Requests whose key comes from their own content are remembered for good. Nothing to do.
How long Clawdline remembers that a request already ran after its day of replay has passed, so a very late resend is still refused instead of running twice.
capacityRow.store.receipts.full: A new request of that kind is refused with a try-again-later answer until the oldest record ages out; nothing still in its day is dropped. Wait a moment and send again.
capacityRow.store.receipts.what: Records of recent requests of each kind (sending a message, a voice note, a Board or schedule change, a project edit) kept for a day so a resend after a dropped connection does not happen twice.
capacityRow.store.retention_prune_batch_: This is a per-pass ceiling, not something that fills. Whatever is left is cleared in the next pass a few minutes later. Nothing to do.
The most old records Clawdline clears from one table in one pass, so clearing a long history never holds up other work.
capacityRow.terminal.body_bytes.full: This is a ceiling on one request, not something that fills up. A larger one is refused as too large and nothing is typed; paste a long text in smaller pieces.
capacityRow.terminal.body_bytes.what: The largest single terminal request this machine accepts from a browser or paired device, such as typed keys or a paste; the biggest legitimate one is a full-size paste. It stops one oversized upload from tying up memory before it is checked.
capacityRow.terminal.count.full: Opening another is refused with a message that the machine already has the maximum open. Close a terminal you no longer need, then open again; Clawdline never closes one for you.
capacityRow.terminal.count.what: How many terminals can be open at once in Clawdline's terminal view on this machine. Each one is a real running shell, so this keeps forgotten shells from piling up and using memory.
capacityRow.terminal.history_lines.full: Asking for more returns only the newest lines; older output is still kept by tmux, just not sent. Nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.terminal.history_lines.what: How many lines of a terminal's earlier output one history read brings back. It keeps one read from sending a terminal's whole scrollback to a phone.
capacityRow.terminal.input_bytes.full: The page already splits what you type into batches that fit, so you will not notice it. A batch that was too large would be refused with nothing typed.
capacityRow.terminal.input_bytes.what: How many keystrokes one send to a terminal may carry. Small batches keep typing responsive and stop one request from pushing a flood of input into the shell.
capacityRow.terminal.lane.full: Further input is turned away as busy with nothing typed, and the page resends the same keystrokes by itself. You may notice a short delay; nothing for you to do.
capacityRow.terminal.lane.what: How many keystroke batches and pastes, across all open terminals, can be in progress or waiting at once. Terminals have their own allowance apart from the assistants' Sessions, so heavy typing cannot slow conversations down.
capacityRow.terminal.launch_line_bytes.f: This is a ceiling on one line. A longer command is saved to a small script and a short line that runs it is typed instead; the assistant starts normally. Only the shell history shows that script's path.
